description_full: Bio-Rad Laboratories, Inc. develops, manufactures, and distributes life science research and clinical diagnostic products in the United States, Europe, Asia, Canada, Latin America, and internationally. It operates through two segments, Life Science and Clinical Diagnostics. The Life Science segment develops, manufactures, and markets instruments, systems, reagents, and consumables to separate, purify, characterize, and quantify biological materials, including cells, proteins, and nucleic acids used in research and biopharmaceutical laboratory environments, as well as for biopharmaceutical manufacturing, quality control process, food safety, and science education applications. This segment serves universities and medical schools, industrial research organizations, government agencies, pharmaceutical manufacturers, biotechnology companies, food producers, and testing laboratories. Its Clinical Diagnostics segment designs, manufactures, markets, and supports diagnostic test systems, informatics systems, test kits, and specialized quality controls for clinical, hospital, diagnostic reference, and transfusion and physician office laboratories, as well as software. The company offers its products through its direct commercial organization, as well as through distributors, agents, brokers, and resellers. Bio-Rad Laboratories, Inc. was founded in 1952 and is headquartered in Hercules, California.

financial_summary: Bio-Rad Laboratories, Inc. is a mid-cap healthcare business with a $9.7B market cap on $2.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -3% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 3% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 55% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $375M in free cash flow — roughly 15 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.70× cash conversion.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 1.0× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 3.0% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 16% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.2× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
